title: Trump: FBI abuses NSA tool to get BLM protesters' emails, text messages
description_short: Trump: FBI abuses NSA tool to get BLM protesters' emails, text messages
description_medium: An account alleged that, in late June 2020, the FBI sought emails, texts, or other communications belonging to people arrested at Black Lives Matter protests by using a Section 702 intelligence tool. The supplied material does not include query records, the legal authority invoked, or a finding by an oversight body. It therefore does not establish that the searches occurred or violated intelligence law.
description_long: The supplied account alleges that the FBI tried to obtain digital communications from Americans arrested at Black Lives Matter demonstrations in late June 2020. It describes the effort as involving Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, a surveillance authority used to collect foreign intelligence about people outside the United States. The record does not identify the exact date, the people affected, the communications sought, or any FBI query documentation. Nor does it provide the legal analysis or oversight findings needed to determine whether the authority was used unlawfully. The episode can therefore be described only as an allegation about intelligence collection connected to protest arrests; the available material does not establish the scope, execution, or legality of any search.

title: Trump: The Justice Dept. becomes Trump's personal legal team
description_short: Trump: The Justice Dept. becomes Trump's personal legal team
description_medium: In September 2020, Attorney General William Barr’s Justice Department sought to take over the federal defense of Donald Trump in E. Jean Carroll’s defamation case. Carroll had sued after Trump publicly called her a liar and attacked her credibility when she accused him of rape. Trump’s lawyers separately sought a delay over their finances, which a judge denied. The federal intervention raised questions about when presidential conduct is treated as official government business.
description_long: In September 2020, Attorney General William Barr’s Justice Department sought to place the federal government in charge of defending Donald Trump against E. Jean Carroll’s defamation suit. Carroll had accused Trump of raping her in a department-store fitting room in the 1990s. She sued for defamation after Trump publicly called her a liar and attacked her credibility; the suit concerned those statements, not a criminal prosecution of the alleged assault. Trump’s personal legal team had separately asked a judge to delay the case, citing financial strain, and the judge denied that request. Barr’s position was that Trump had been acting as president when he made the statements, an argument that would shift the defense from his personal lawyers to the government. The move drew scrutiny because it invoked federal authority in a personal defamation dispute. A jury later found for Carroll in a related trial and awarded her $5 million in 2023. The supplied account does not treat that later verdict as a ruling on every issue raised by the Justice Department’s attempted intervention.

title: Trump: News leaks that former Trump Campaign manager is writing a tell-all book
description_short: Trump: News leaks that former Trump Campaign manager is writing a tell-all book
description_medium: Reports attributed to people close to Donald Trump said former campaign manager Brad Parscale was writing a tell-all book after his departure from the 2020 campaign. The New York Times’ Maggie Haberman reported that the prospect unsettled Trump’s team. The supplied account said Parscale was among those who had not signed a nondisclosure agreement, but it does not confirm a manuscript, publisher, or eventual book.
description_long: The report concerned a possible book by Brad Parscale, who had managed Donald Trump’s 2020 campaign before being replaced. The supplied account, citing New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman and unnamed people close to Trump, said Parscale was writing a tell-all and that the prospect had left the Trump team “rattled.” It also said Parscale was believed to be among campaign figures who had not signed a nondisclosure agreement. These details describe a reported plan, not a completed publication: the record names no publisher, manuscript, release date, or contents of a book. Parscale’s former campaign role helps explain why the rumor attracted attention, but the available material does not show that he disclosed campaign information or that any particular account appeared in print. The event is therefore the reporting of a potential insider book and the reaction attributed to Trump’s circle, rather than proof that a tell-all was written or published.

title: Trump: ICE tries forcing journalists to reveal anonymous sources
description_short: Trump: ICE tries forcing journalists to reveal anonymous sources
description_medium: Between November 30 and December 4, 2020, Immigration and Customs Enforcement issued BuzzFeed News a subpoena seeking the identities of confidential sources. Editor-in-chief Mark Schoofs said the newsroom would not identify sources or discuss its reporting methods and called the demand an overreach. The account places the subpoena within a broader effort to identify government whistleblowers and people who leaked documents.
description_long: In late November or early December 2020, Immigration and Customs Enforcement subpoenaed BuzzFeed News for information that could identify its confidential sources. The linked account places the demand between November 30 and December 4. Editor-in-chief Mark Schoofs said BuzzFeed would not confirm or discuss confidential sources or reporting methods, and argued that the subpoena was incompatible with the Constitution and would not affect its journalism. The account described the request as part of a broader Trump-administration effort to identify whistleblowers and people who had leaked government documents. David Snyder of the First Amendment Coalition warned that compelling journalists to disclose sources or reporting information could weaken journalism’s ability to support public accountability. The supplied material does not state what underlying story or records ICE sought, whether BuzzFeed challenged the subpoena in court, or how the demand was ultimately resolved. It does document a direct conflict between a federal agency’s demand for source-identifying information and a newsroom’s stated commitment to confidentiality.
